title: Diastasis Recti Surgery: When a Tummy Tuck Repairs It
meta_description: Diastasis recti surgery is usually a tummy tuck with muscle repair. How to check for a gap, when physical therapy comes first and what insurance covers.
excerpt: Diastasis recti surgery is usually a tummy tuck with muscle repair. Here is how to check for a gap, when physical therapy comes first, what insurance covers and how often the gap comes back, with the evidence stated plainly.
quick_answer:
Does a tummy tuck fix diastasis recti?

Usually, when the surgery includes muscle repair. ASPS describes a tummy tuck as restoring weakened or separated muscles in most cases. Cleveland Clinic says diastasis recti affects 6 in 10 women after childbirth, counts a gap wider than 2 centimeters, and suggests working with a physical therapist. Skin-only surgery does not close the gap.

How to check for a gap at home

Lie on your back with your knees bent and your feet flat on the floor
Lift your shoulders slightly off the ground, keeping one hand behind your head
Put your other hand above your belly button, palm down and fingers toward your toes
Feel for a gap between your stomach muscles and count how many fingers fit

Two or more finger widths: talk to your healthcare provider

Source: Cleveland Clinic

sources.title: Diastasis Recti (last updated 04/21/2025)
quotes: It’s a common condition that affects 6 in 10 women after childbirth.
An abdominal gap wider than 2 centimeters is considered diastasis recti.
The rectus abdominis is divided into left and right sides by a band of tissue called the linea alba.
As your uterus expands during pregnancy, your linea alba thins and pulls apart.
A visible bulge or “pooch” that protrudes just above or below your belly button (even after losing any weight you may have gained during pregnancy)
Coning or doming when you contract your ab muscles or lean back in a chair
Diastasis recti isn’t painful. You may feel pain due to some of the side effects of diastasis, but the ab separation itself doesn’t hurt.
Diastasis recti can occur above your belly button, below your belly button and at your belly button
Some providers may use ultrasound, measuring tape or a tool called a caliper for a more accurate measurement.
Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor.
Lift your shoulders slightly off the ground, keeping one hand behind your head for support, almost like you are doing a sit-up.
Move your other hand above your belly button area, palms down and fingers towards your toes.
If you feel a gap of two or more finger widths, discuss your concerns with your healthcare provider.
Work with a physical therapist who has experience with diastasis recti.
Yes, it’s possible to fix diastasis recti without surgery.
They might do surgery if you have an umbilical hernia or if you want diastasis recti surgery (a tummy tuck).
mild cases with a little separation may improve with minimal effort
Most diastasis recti exercises involve deep breathing and slow, controlled movements.
Planks or push-ups (unless using modifications)
Wearing binders can’t heal diastasis recti and won’t strengthen your core muscles.
If you have more than a two-finger gap between your abdominals or are experiencing pain, contact your healthcare provider for a diagnosis.
Men can get it from excessive or chronic straining. Things like lifting heavy weights, constipation or sudden weight gain/weight loss can contribute to men getting diastasis.
Crunches or sit-ups of any kind

sources.title: Diastasis recti repair: Restoring core strength and abdominal integrity (September 22, 2025)
quotes: We most often do it as part of an abdominoplasty (tummy tuck) – it's actually an integral part of a tummy tuck.

We'll do a low transverse incision, which allows us to access the abdominal wall and remove the excess skin and fat in the lower belly. At the same time, we use surgery and sutures to reposition and repair the diastasis recti.

However, this does not give a solution to people, particularly women, who don't have a lot of skin and fat in their lower belly but still suffer from diastasis recti. To address this issue, there have been laparoscopic and robotic techniques that have been developed, allowing you to repair it from inside the abdomen. For us, I generally do this in cooperation with a general surgeon
And very often, this is also done in conjunction with hernia repairs.
I am not aware of any nonsurgical techniques that can effectively repair diastasis recti.

The ideal candidate is someone who feels like they want this surgery and is also at or near their goal weight or a healthy weight. If you're very large or overweight and you carry a lot of extra fatty tissue around your organs, it will limit our ability to repair the diastasis.
This is a surgery that requires real recovery. I usually tell women to expect up to two weeks out of work.
You could have a sensation of tightness, but that should improve over time.
it can also occur in both men and women due to weight fluctuations, abdominal surgeries and improper exercise techniques.
Obviously, a rare complication is an injury to intra-abdominal structures. That's why it's important to have a multidisciplinary surgical team.

notes: Retargeted from 'Tummy Tuck Diastasis Recti Miami: Restore Your Core' under issue #357, reversing the fold in the 2026-10-05 plan. About half the post's named impressions were Miami head terms that belong to the page. Written fresh for readers deciding. Removed: Miami targeting in title, headings and body; double board-certified, AAAASF, 20 years and 4.9 rating claims; phone number; financing terms; '60% ... 32.6-45.4%'; 'gold standard'; 'BMI under 30' attributed to Cleveland Clinic; 'Mayo Clinic notes'; 'rarely closes gaps wider than two centimeters'; 'lifelong strength'; 'reduced back pain within weeks'; 2-5 hours; 6-8 weeks of lifting; humidity and swelling; all first-person voice. Sources: the review the brief names (PMC7839807) is Gormley and colleagues, Cureus, published 29 Dec 2020, so the post says 2020, not the plan's 2021. What it says on recurrence, read in full text: it did not analyze recurrence as such; its Introduction says 'the recurrence rate of ARD has been reported as high as 40% [3]', where [3] is Hickey 2011, and its Table 5 lists 1 ARD recurrence in Emanuelsson. The post attributes it that way and doesn't present 40% as that review's finding. To answer 'Will it come back?' honestly I also read the abstracts of Swedenhammar 2021, Nahas 2005, de Castro 2013, van Uchelen 2001, Hickey 2011 and Emanuelsson 2016: no recurrence to 40%, small studies, no direct absorbable vs nonabsorbable comparison among them. Whether Hickey's 40% comes from van Uchelen is not stated in the abstract, so the post doesn't claim it. Exercise evidence added beyond the card: Benjamin 2023 and Emanuelsson 2016. Sources that disagree are shown as disagreeing: Cleveland Clinic ('possible to fix without surgery') vs Tomer Avraham, MD ('not aware of any nonsurgical techniques'); ASPS on insurance vs Frank Campanile, MD ('should be covered, at least in part'); 2 centimeters (Cleveland Clinic) vs 2.7 centimeters (Campanile). Avraham and Campanile are attributed by name: the ASPS article is a freelance writer's interview, the post is the author's view. The ASPS insurance sentence is from the cost page. The Avraham line on hernia repair sits in his answer on laparoscopic and robotic repair, so the post places it there. Nothing says which technique, sutures or hernia and laparoscopic options the practice offers: owner questions, stated as questions to ask. The mini and extended mini lines come from the facts file (the price sheet says no muscle repair). No price appears; the post links #pricing. FAQ 'does it cost more' is link only. Live FAQs kept in spirit: exercise, Ozempic; recovery and risks moved to the body. Figures not in tummy-tuck.facts.ts have their own quotes here: 0.43 cm, 16 trials and 698 women, 3-month program, 81.25%, 7 studies and 497 patients, 17.0% of 276, 94.4%, 2.7 cm, 12 months, up to a full year, and the recurrence table. Deviations from the card: the mini vs full and pregnancy posts (N3, N1) are not linked because they ship in Batch 3 and this post ships in Batch 1, so a link would 404 until then; the page's #which-tummy-tuck and #recovery carry those readers. Add both links when Batch 3 goes live. Images: all 6 live images are retired (hero alt 'sculpted flat abdomen', one shows the surgeon, old infographics carry old figures). New set: hero + 4 inline. The separation image carries same_address_url, the live rectus diagram (blog-images/1a95b26e.../1768920607327-u20y88-0.jpg, 168 image impressions): plan section 6 replaces it at the same address only after the canary passes, using overwrite_same_path.mjs. That key is a note for the main session; the kit ignores it, and export_upload.mjs would otherwise give a new URL. The registry entry still lists 'tummy tuck diastasis recti miami' strings in ownsQueries; they are left out of owns_queries here. Sources were read as text with curl (PubMed through eutils) on 2026-11-03, the ASPS article also through WebFetch, and every quote was machine-checked against that text. Fact-check of 4 Nov applied (factcheck/scar-diastasis.md, plus the pregnancy wording from factcheck/new-posts.md): Emanuelsson randomized between two repairs with training as a control followed for 3 months, not surgery against training; the Swedenhammar row is the same cohort with its one early recurrence excluded before the 5-year count (full text PMC8551425); 'newborns' replaces 'babies' to match the abstract's 'neonatal'; Cheng 2024 added for preterm delivery; Hickey's 'largely cosmetic' conclusion added.
